entries.clue: It could be rock, marble or maybe even mud?! (4)

annotation.definition: It could be rock, marble or maybe even mud?!

blocks.note: the surface offers two things a quarry cuts, hard materials you might build or carve with
mud is the one nobody builds with, and the exclamation mark is the setter enjoying the moment the list stops being geology

annotation.surface: Someone guessing what an unidentified lump of material might turn out to be made of.
annotation.walkthrough: Rock and marble keep company as things a quarry cuts, and mud is the one that will not sit with them, which is the tell. The tea-room shelf, not the stoneyard, is where all three turn up together.
annotation.definitionFit: All three name a kind of cake — the currant-studded rock cake, the marbled sponge, the chocolate mud cake — so the odd list is one baker's shelf.

entries.clue: Lifted part of chrysalid off a dying flower (8)

indicatorNotes.Lifted: In a down entry anything lifted travels up the column, so the run of letters is read from its foot back to its head.
indicatorNotes.part of: Part of something is a stretch taken out of the middle of it, which is where these letters are sitting.

blocks.note: the run chrysa-LID OFF A D-ying, eight consecutive letters read back up the column

annotation.surface: Part of a chrysalis being lifted off a flower that is on its way out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A dying flower' reads as one sad phrase and is two jobs: 'dying' hands over the D the run ends on, and only the last word defines. A chrysalid is the pupa a caterpillar shuts itself into.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the trumpeted yellow bloom of early spring is one flower among many, and the clue is content with the general word.

entries.clue: Cwm venue cleared out to welcome everyone back from Hay (6)

indicatorNotes.cleared out: A room cleared out has had everything between its walls removed, so the word keeps only the letters at its two ends.
indicatorNotes.to welcome: To welcome people is to take them in through your door, so they end up inside rather than alongside.
indicatorNotes.back: The back of a word is the end of it, and that final letter is all this asks for.

blocks.note: VENUE emptied of everything between its first and last letters
everyone there is all of them
the back letter of Hay, the book-festival town on the Welsh border

annotation.surface: A stripped-out venue at Hay making room to welcome the whole crowd back again.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Everyone back' looks like an instruction to turn a word round, and it is nothing of the sort: the back belongs to Hay, three words further on. Cwm is Welsh, and the puzzle is full of Wales.
annotation.definitionFit: Cwm is the Welsh word, long since naturalised in English, for the steep-sided hollow between hills that a stream runs down.

entries.clue: After capsizing, criticise involving fat swimmers (8)

indicatorNotes.After capsizing: A capsized boat has gone completely over, and in a down entry letters turned that way are read up the column instead of down.
indicatorNotes.involving: To involve someone is to draw them into the middle of the business, so these letters sit inside the others.

blocks.note: to criticise is to slam, and SLAM turned upside down reads this way
lard is the fat rendered from a pig

annotation.surface: After the boat goes over, someone finds time to criticise the overweight swimmers.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface puts people in the water, so 'swimmers' is read as bathers rather than as anything with feathers. Lard for fat and slam for criticise are both worth filing away.
annotation.definitionFit: The commonest wild duck of every British pond spends its life on the water, so 'swimmers' takes the birds by what they do.

entries.clue: Doctor – in the past Neath’s top fire-breather (6)

indicatorNotes.top: In a down entry the top is where the word starts, so only its first letter is taken.

blocks.note: the two letters on any doctor's brass plate
something in the past happened a while ago
the first letter of Neath, a town in south Wales

annotation.surface: A doctor who was once the leading fire-eater in Neath.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is the setter's favourite word for shuffling letters, and here it does nothing of the kind — it is two letters taken at face value. The red beast on the Welsh flag is the one being described.
annotation.definitionFit: The beast of legend is known above all for the flame it breathes, so the hyphenated description names it by its one famous trick.

entries.clue: Drink and drugs masking onset of rheumatism (4)

indicatorNotes.masking: To mask a thing is to cover it over, so what is named next disappears inside the letters named before.
indicatorNotes.onset of: The onset of something is the moment it begins, and a word begins with its first letter.

blocks.note: pot is the oldest slang for cannabis, and the word opens after its second letter
the letter rheumatism starts with

annotation.surface: Drink and drugs hiding the first signs of rheumatism in somebody.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drink and drugs' is such a fixed pairing that the eye takes it as one phrase, and the little word between them is doing the joining: the first is the definition, the second is wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Port is the sweet fortified red passed round after dinner, so the general word takes it as one drink among many.

entries.clue: Rolling pad? (7)

blocks.note: the surface suggests rolling country or a rolling gait; the setter means running along on its own wheels
pad is slang for the place you live, and the question mark admits it is a dwelling of a very particular sort

annotation.walkthrough: A pad is where you live, the slang of anyone who has had a flat, and the joke is that this one is towed. Two words and a question mark is the whole clue, so all of it has to be read twice.
annotation.definitionFit: A caravan is a home on wheels, so it is a pad in the slang sense and a rolling one in the literal sense at the same time.

entries.clue: Country lover in threesome caught by postman (7)

indicatorNotes.caught by: Anything caught by someone is held fast in their grip, so it ends up enclosed by the letters named after it.

blocks.note: Postman Pat, the children's television postman every British household knows, and the name opens after its second letter
three musicians playing together are a trio

annotation.surface: A tabloid item: a country music fan caught in a threesome by the man delivering the post.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a scandal sheet, which is what makes 'country lover' read as a taste in music or in scenery rather than as devotion to a flag.
annotation.definitionFit: A patriot's whole character is love of their own country, so the two words are meant straight, with 'lover' left to look like the tabloid kind.

entries.clue: Will the author flog incomplete bit of fiction? (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition names a man instead of describing a thing: given his first name and his trade, the answer is the surname that completes him.

indicatorNotes.incomplete: Something incomplete stops before it should, so the word is written out a letter short.
indicatorNotes.bit of: A bit of a word is a fragment of it, and the fragment a clue takes without further explanation is the letter it starts with.

blocks.note: to flog something is to sell it, cut short of its last letter
the letter fiction begins with

annotation.surface: Asking whether the writer intends to sell off an unfinished piece of made-up work.
annotation.walkthrough: The opening word looks like the auxiliary that starts any question, and it is a first name: Will Self is a London novelist, and the question mark is the setter pointing at him.
annotation.definitionFit: Will Self is a British novelist, so naming him by first name and calling leaves the surname for the solver to supply.

entries.clue: Artificial glow in hole, naked flame ahead (9)

indicatorNotes.naked: Naked is stripped of everything worn on the outside, so the word loses the letters at either end and keeps its middle.
indicatorNotes.ahead: Ahead is in front, so the piece just named is written before the other one.

blocks.note: FLAME with the letters at its two ends taken off
to be in a hole is to be in a plight, both of them awkward spots to be in

annotation.surface: A man-made glow down a hole, with an uncovered flame burning in front of it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Naked flame' is the phrase off every safety notice, which is why it reads as one thing rather than as an instruction and the word it applies to. A hole meaning a plight is the other half of the trap.
annotation.definitionFit: Light shed by a lamp is made by people rather than by the sun or a fire, which is a glow that is artificial.

entries.clue: Stifled complaints when flashy jewellery confiscated by parents (9)

indicatorNotes.confiscated by: What is confiscated is taken off you and shut away by somebody else, so these letters end up locked inside the others.

blocks.note: mums are parents, and the word opens after its third letter
bling is the slang for showy gold and diamonds worn to be noticed

annotation.surface: A teenager grumbling under their breath while mum and dad take the flashy jewellery away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Parents' asks for mothers only, a part of the group standing in for the whole, which is licence every setter takes. The surface and the answer describe the same sulky evening.
annotation.definitionFit: A mumbling is a complaint that never gets past the lips — audible but not articulated — which is precisely a complaint stifled.

entries.clue: Backs off homeward rapidly after scoundrel leaves box? (5)

annotation.definitionNote: 'Leaves box' is not a dictionary phrase but a description built on the spot, which is what the question mark owns; the leaves are tea.

indicatorNotes.Backs off: The back of a word is its last letter, and taking the backs off two words leaves exactly those two letters.
indicatorNotes.after: After places the piece just named behind the one described next, so it comes second in the finished answer.

blocks.note: a cad is a scoundrel, the old word for a man who treats people badly
the last letter of each word, in the order the clue gives them

annotation.surface: Everyone retreating fast towards home once the scoundrel has taken himself off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scoundrel leaves' reads as one departure, and the second word has jumped the fence into the definition: what is boxed here is tea. The small lidded tin on the kitchen shelf is the thing meant.
annotation.definitionFit: A tea caddy is the lidded box the dry leaves are kept in, so calling it a leaves box describes it exactly, if not in so many dictionary words.

entries.clue: Players receiving nothing for progress without much effort (5)

indicatorNotes.receiving: To receive something is to take it in, so the letter named next is admitted inside.

blocks.note: the players in a production are its cast, and the word opens after its first letter
nothing is the round O of a nought on a scoresheet

annotation.surface: Actors being paid nothing for work that costs them very little effort.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Players' wants to be footballers or a band, and it is the theatre sense that pays. O for nothing is one of the first conventions to learn.
annotation.definitionFit: A cyclist who coasts keeps rolling on momentum alone, pedalling not at all, so to coast is to get along with almost no effort spent.

entries.clue: Ran over, captivated by Tony’s forbidden sweetheart, saucy thing! (8)

annotation.definitionNote: Saucy normally means cheeky, and the setter is using it in the literal sense of 'being a sauce', which the exclamation mark owns.

indicatorNotes.over: Turned over, a word lies the other way up, so the letters just named are written from last to first.
indicatorNotes.captivated by: To captivate somebody is to hold them captive, and a captive is kept shut inside.

blocks.note: in West Side Story Tony loves Maria, whose family runs the rival gang, so the two of them are forbidden each other
RAN written the other way round

annotation.surface: A driver runs somebody over, spellbound by Tony's off-limits girlfriend.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ran over' is a road accident on the surface and a three-letter word turned round underneath. The tomato-and-garlic sauce takes its name from sailors, alla marinara meaning in the mariner's style.
annotation.definitionFit: Marinara is the plain tomato, garlic and oregano sauce of Italian kitchens, so it is a thing made of sauce, with cheekiness the decoy.

entries.clue: Sport wig, covering for baldy (5)

indicatorNotes.covering for: A covering goes round the outside of a thing, so what is taken is the letters at the two ends and nothing in between.

blocks.note: a rug is a toupee, the wig worn over a bald patch
the outside letters of the word, the ones covering it at each end

annotation.surface: Wearing a wig to cover up a bald head.
annotation.walkthrough: The first word reads as a verb, to sport a wig, and it is the definition standing on its own as a noun. Rug for wig is a small piece of slang the setter expects you to have.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the fifteen-a-side game the Welsh national side plays is one sport, and the clue names only the category.

entries.clue: Draw is as much as bowler can take, perhaps, losing heart (4)

indicatorNotes.perhaps: Perhaps offers the thing named as one example of something wider, so it is a hat in general whose capacity is being measured.
indicatorNotes.losing heart: The heart of a word is the letters at its dead centre, and losing them closes the two ends up together.

blocks.clueFragment: as much as bowler can take
blocks.note: a bowler is a hat, and a hatful is as much as one will hold; the middle two letters then go

annotation.surface: A cricket match ending level is all the bowler can manage once the spirit has gone out of him.
annotation.walkthrough: Draw and bowler both belong to cricket, which is where the sentence wants you, and the bowler here is the stiff black hat of a City gent. Six letters lose their middle pair.
annotation.definitionFit: To haul is to pull something heavy along, and to draw a cart or a curtain is the same action under another verb.

entries.clue: Nation with beer – ultimately Brains (5)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: Ultimately means at the very end of things, so what is wanted is the last letter of the word.

blocks.note: w is the everyday short form of with, as in w/ on a scribbled note
ale is beer
the last letter of Brains, the Cardiff brewery whose bitter the surface is ordering

annotation.surface: A country and a beer, with Brains the last word on the subject.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics dress the final word as a name, and it is a name: SA Brain of Cardiff have been brewing since 1882, so every word of the surface is as Welsh as the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: one of the four nations of the United Kingdom is being asked for by its category alone.

entries.clue: Odd lawn cultivated around old group of trees (8)

indicatorNotes.cultivated: Cultivated ground has been dug over and worked, and letters worked over like that come out in a different order.
indicatorNotes.around: What goes around a thing encircles it, so the letters already made open up and take the next one inside.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, seven letters
o is the standard abbreviation for old, dropped in among the rearranged letters

annotation.surface: An unusual lawn laid out around an old clump of trees.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Odd' in front of a word normally asks for its alternate letters; here it is plain fodder and the gardening word does the shuffling. The single letter for old drops in once the rest has been rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: Woodland is country under growing trees, which is what a group of trees becomes when it is left long enough to spread.

entries.clue: Hutch, partner to Lacey, leaving New York (4)

indicatorNotes.leaving: Leaving is going away for good, so the letters named next walk out of the word and what remains closes up.

blocks.note: Cagney and Lacey were the two New York detectives of the 1980s television series
NY is the state's postal abbreviation, and these are the two letters that go

annotation.surface: Hutch, the man who partnered Lacey, getting himself out of New York.
annotation.walkthrough: Hutch belongs to Starsky in everybody's memory, and the setter is banking on it: here it is the wire-fronted box at the bottom of the garden. The two letters that leave are the ones the detectives worked in.
annotation.definitionFit: A hutch is the boxed enclosure a rabbit or ferret is kept in, which is a cage under a homelier name.

entries.clue: Dressing up Cain with drag clothing (8)

indicatorNotes.Dressing up: To dress up is to put on a disguise, and letters in disguise are not left in the order they were handed over in.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters, the little word in the middle joining the two halves

annotation.surface: Cain got up in drag, wearing somebody else's frock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dressing' opens the clue wanting to be the definition, and the definition is the last word instead. Drag is the sort of word that usually pulls letters about, and here it is fodder. Cardigan is also a town on the west Welsh coast.
annotation.definitionFit: A cardigan is the knitted wool jacket that buttons up the front, so it is clothing plain and simple.

entries.clue: Resign, depressed after returning beloved animals (4,4)

indicatorNotes.after: After puts the piece just named behind the one described next, so it comes second in the finished phrase.
indicatorNotes.returning: Something returning is on its way back the way it came, so those letters are read from the end to the start.

blocks.note: beloved animals are pets, and PETS sent back the way it came reads this way
somebody depressed is down

annotation.surface: Somebody quits, low in spirits, after taking their much-loved animals back.
annotation.walkthrough: Returning animals is a real and miserable thing to do, which is why the word never looks like an instruction. The phrase is the one every chairman's resignation statement reaches for.
annotation.definitionFit: To step down is to give up an office or a post voluntarily, which is what resigning is.

entries.clue: Crime quick, taking in Inland Revenue (6)

indicatorNotes.taking in: To take somebody in is to admit them indoors, so the letters named next go inside the word before.

blocks.note: something quick is pacy, and the word opens after its first letter
IR was the Inland Revenue, the British tax collector now folded into HMRC

annotation.surface: A crime carried out in a hurry, with the taxman brought in on it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crime quick' reads as a headline with the verb missing, and the two words have nothing to do with each other: the first defines and the second builds. A quick temper and a pacy thriller share the same adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: Piracy is a crime twice over — robbery on the high seas, and the copying of other people's films and songs — so the bare word covers it.

entries.clue: Clichéd rabbit straddling lover’s rear (5)

indicatorNotes.straddling: To straddle a thing is to stand over it with a leg each side, which puts it squarely in the middle.
indicatorNotes.rear: The rear of a word is its back end, so the final letter is all that is taken.

blocks.note: a cony is a rabbit, the old name that survives in the fur trade, and the word opens after its second letter
the rear letter of lover

annotation.surface: A rabbit mounted on its mate's back end, as rabbits are always said to be.
annotation.walkthrough: In crosswords 'rabbit' usually means to talk, from the rhyming slang rabbit and pork, so the animal itself is the surprise. Cony is the older spelling and the one setters keep alive.
annotation.definitionFit: A corny joke or sentiment is one worn smooth by too much use, which is exactly what calling something clichéd says about it.

entries.clue: Shy exhausted little rook? (6)

indicatorNotes.exhausted: Something exhausted has had everything taken out of it and is left as a shell, which for a word is its first and last letters.

blocks.note: to shy a stone at something is to cast it
the word emptied out, keeping only the letters at its two ends

annotation.surface: A timid little rook worn out from a day on the wing.
annotation.walkthrough: Shy reads as bashful and means to throw, the sense left in a coconut shy at a fairground. The bird in the surface is a corvid; the one in the definition stands in the corner of a chessboard.
annotation.definitionFit: The corner piece in chess goes by two names, rook and castle, so either word names the other straight across.

entries.clue: Those out-of-town rush trails – rambling but not hard (9)

indicatorNotes.rambling: A rambling walk wanders about with no fixed route, and letters that ramble do not stay in the order they were given.
indicatorNotes.but not: But not marks something the sentence has to do without, so that letter is taken out before the rest is worked on.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters, one of which is about to go
H is the hard of a pencil grade, and it is the letter dropped from the fodder

annotation.surface: Out-of-town running trails that wander a good deal but are not hard going.
annotation.walkthrough: Rambling is exactly what you do on a country trail, which is why it never looks like an instruction, and a walk that is not hard is the same sentence read straight. A ruralist is someone who chooses country life.
annotation.definitionFit: Ruralists live out in the country by preference, so 'those out-of-town' names the same people as a townsman would.

entries.clue: Big Bird runs, hearty, but half-cut (4)

indicatorNotes.half-cut: Half-cut is half of it cut away, so only the front half of the word's letters is left standing.

blocks.note: r is runs on a cricket scorecard
the first half of the six letters, the back half cut off

annotation.surface: A large bird running about, cheerful enough but rather the worse for drink.
annotation.walkthrough: Half-cut means tipsy, which is what keeps it in the surface, and the capital letters point at the yellow one on Sesame Street. The bird actually wanted is the South American cousin of the ostrich, flightless and fast on its feet.
annotation.definitionFit: A rhea stands shoulder-high to a person and cannot fly, so big bird describes it flatly, whatever the capitals suggest.

entries.clue: Maybe Skye lies elaborately (4)

indicatorNotes.elaborately: To do a thing elaborately is to work it up into something more complicated, and letters worked over that way come out in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, four letters

annotation.surface: A girl called Skye telling the most elaborate untruths.
annotation.walkthrough: The four letters mean untruths on the surface and, of a place, where it sits: Skye lies off the west coast. Both senses are in play at once, and only one of them is doing any work.
annotation.definitionFit: Skye is one of the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland, and 'maybe' offers it as one example of the thing wanted.

entries.clue: National emblem in France, the ‘Disheartened Deer’ (4)

indicatorNotes.Disheartened: Disheartened is heartless, so the letter sitting at the very centre of the word has gone.

blocks.note: le is the French for 'the'
an elk is a deer, and ELK loses the letter at its heart

annotation.surface: A national emblem in France, known as the 'Disheartened Deer'.
annotation.walkthrough: France sends you hunting for the cockerel, and all it supplies is the French word for 'the'. The vegetable meant is worn on St David's Day and stitched on the shirt of the Welsh rugby side.
annotation.definitionFit: The leek is the badge of Wales, as the rose is England's and the thistle Scotland's.

entries.clue: Warnings of danger from almost defeated Tories (7)

indicatorNotes.almost: Almost stops just short of the whole, so the word is written out with its last letter missing.

blocks.note: defeated is beaten, stopped a letter short of the end
Cons is the newspapers' short form for Conservatives on any election night

annotation.surface: Danger signals coming from Tory members who were very nearly beaten at the polls.
annotation.walkthrough: Beacons were the hilltop fires lit in a chain to tell the country an invasion was coming, which is what makes them warnings and not merely lights. The Brecon ones keep this puzzle's Welsh company.
annotation.definitionFit: A beacon is a fire or light set high up to signal that trouble is on its way, so a row of them is a set of warnings.

entries.clue: Sounded like a sheep audible at Edgbaston trapped inside somewhere? (7)

indicatorNotes.trapped inside somewhere: Something trapped inside somewhere is shut in and out of view, and these letters are shut inside the words standing next to them.

blocks.note: the run starts partway through the first word, crosses the second whole and takes the first letter of the third

annotation.surface: A sheep shut in somewhere near the ground, loud enough to be heard by the crowd at Edgbaston.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Audible' is the word every solver reads as an instruction to listen for a sound-alike, and it is fodder. Edgbaston is the Birmingham cricket ground, which is why a sheep there is worth remarking on.
annotation.definitionFit: To bleat is to make the thin wavering cry of a sheep, so anything that bleated sounded exactly like one.
